title: Gemini Notebook: A Source-Checked Workflow for Comparing Software Quotes
content:
Quick answer: Gemini Notebook, previously called NotebookLM, is worth trying when you need to answer a question from a small set of documents. Start with its currently free Standard tier, but do not confuse source-grounded answers with guaranteed accuracy or permanent free access.

Updated 8 October 2026. Documentation-based guide, not a hands-on test. The example below is hypothetical; it uses no confidential customer material.

What changed, and what did not

Google announced the rename to Gemini Notebook on 16 July 2026, with a rollout to personal and Workspace accounts over several weeks. A familiar NotebookLM name in an older guide does not mean it describes a different product.

The official plan page currently offers Standard free of charge. Limits, feature access and availability can change. This is not a promise of $0 forever, and paid plans should be checked for both features and usage limits before you buy.

A practical use case: compare two software proposals

Imagine a US or UK freelancer choosing a project-management service. One vendor quotes per user, another per workspace; annual discounts make the monthly headline misleading. Rather than ask a chatbot which product is best, use the proposals to find the missing information.

  1. Check permission before uploading. Use public proposals or documents you are authorised to share. Do not upload a client contract, employee data or credentials just because the tool is free. Check your organisation's requirements and the terms for the account you use.
  2. Create a narrowly scoped notebook. Name it for one decision, not your entire business. Add the two current proposals and, if permitted, your own requirements note.
  3. Label the sources. Include vendor, document date, currency and billing period in your notes. A dollar figure from a US page is not a UK pound price. Check tax treatment in the quote rather than assuming VAT or sales tax is included.
  4. Ask for facts, gaps and citations separately. Tell the notebook not to fill missing fields from general knowledge.
  5. Open each cited passage. Confirm the price basis, minimum seats, cancellation terms and renewal conditions yourself. A citation can point to text that does not support the whole answer.
  6. Ask the vendor about gaps. If the source does not state an export fee, write “not stated,” not “free.” Keep the original documents outside the notebook.

A prompt you can adapt

Using only the selected proposals, compare Vendor A and Vendor B for five users over 12 months. For each item, identify the source: billing currency, monthly versus annual commitment, minimum seats, tax treatment, cancellation terms and data export. Write “not stated” when a proposal does not specify something. Separate facts from assumptions. Do not convert currencies or recommend a winner until the missing terms are resolved.

This is a suggested workflow, not a claim that the product will execute every instruction correctly. The human review is part of the process.

Do the annual-cost arithmetic outside the summary

Suppose a hypothetical offer is £12 per user per month with annual billing and a five-seat minimum. The annual subscription would be £12 × 5 × 12 = £720 before any additional tax or charges. An introductory three-month discount cannot be treated as a permanent rate. If another proposal is in US dollars, compare the contractual terms first and make any currency conversion explicitly dated.

That simple calculation adds more decision value than a broad “best app” ranking. It is deliberately an example, not a current vendor price.

Source-grounded does not mean the whole product is source-only

Google's help documentation describes chat responses based on source data with citations. It also describes uses with or without sources and additional capabilities such as web research. Be clear about which mode and sources you are using.

For an evidence-based memo, stick to the selected material, verify the citations and preserve unresolved questions. Neither a source-grounded notebook nor a general chatbot should be treated as a substitute for reading the decisive contract clause.

Why usage can run out before you expect

Google's usage-limit guidance describes compute-based limits, with allowances refreshing every five hours up to a weekly limit. Workload matters, not just the number of questions. Check your account's current limits rather than relying on an old daily-request figure from a review.

When paying makes sense

Try a small, representative project first. Record what blocks you: the number of sources, a feature you need, or repeated usage limits. Then compare the official plans available for your account and country. Do not upgrade simply because a reviewer quotes a cheap US monthly price.

If you only need one short document summarised occasionally, a new paid subscription may add little. If you cannot upload the material under your organisation's policy, a higher tier does not automatically solve that permission problem.

Before you send the final memo

  • Every important factual claim has a source you opened.
  • Missing details are labelled, not guessed.
  • Currencies and billing periods are explicit.
  • Your recommendation is separate from the vendors' claims.
  • The original documents remain accessible independently of the AI tool.

Correction note: This revision removes the unsupported “$0 forever” promise and the claim that paid plans only increase volume. It also narrows the earlier source-only claim to source-grounded chat and replaces unverified pricing assertions with an auditable worked example.
